nodes.chainStep: Airway and breathing; SpO2 to a target range, with a blood gas if hypoxia or CO2 retention is possible; capillary glucose; full vitals with temperature; GCS
nodes.why: A capillary glucose belongs in the ABCDE of every acutely ill adult, and hypoglycemia must be excluded in anyone with diabetes who is drowsy, unconscious, unable to cooperate, aggressive or seizing; exposure includes the temperature. Unexplained confusion can be the presenting feature of hypoxemia or hypercapnia, so the saturation goes with a blood gas when that is possible. A depressed conscious level is put down to intoxication only after an important brain injury has been excluded. In delirium the first job is the cause; haloperidol comes only for distress or danger, once de-escalation has failed.

nodes.why: For known or suspected opioid overdose the label gives 0.4 to 2 mg IV, repeated every 2 to 3 minutes, IM or subcutaneously when there is no vein, alongside airway support and ventilation; if 10 mg brings no response, the diagnosis is questioned. Some opioids outlast naloxone, so the patient stays under observation for repeat doses, and BTS checks a blood gas for hypercapnia after a respiratory depressant.

nodes.chainStep: Controlled oxygen to 88 to 92%; optimal medical therapy for the exacerbation; repeat the gas; NIV if a pH under 7.35 with a PCO2 over 6.5 kPa persists; invasive ventilation when more appropriate
nodes.why: In acute hypercapnic respiratory failure from a COPD exacerbation, controlled oxygen aims for a saturation of 88 to 92%, neither switched off nor pushed toward normal. NIV starts when a pH under 7.35 with a PCO2 over 6.5 kPa persists or develops despite optimal medical therapy, and must not delay invasive ventilation when that is more appropriate; a GCS under 8 is one of BTS/ICS's indications for invasive ventilation. Naloxone is the antidote for opiate poisoning, not for CO2 narcosis.

nodes.why: Fever, headache, neck stiffness and an altered level of consciousness are NICE's red flag combination for bacterial meningitis, and antibiotics start within 1 hour of arrival; bloods and antibiotics come before any imaging, and dexamethasone goes with or before the first dose without delaying it. results.front: Capillary glucose 5.0 mmol/L (90 mg/dL); GCS 13, protecting the airway; BP 104/66, HR 52, SpO2 94%; bladder temperature 31.2 °C (88.2 °F).
results.clues: Found outdoors in wet clothing overnight; not shivering; no thyroid history or scar, normal reflexes; no alcohol on his breath, no injury, no focal deficit.
